title: Chapter 124 — The Needle
paragraphs: Next morning the not-yet-subsided sea rolled in long, slow billows of mighty bulk, and striving in the Pequod's gurgling track, pushed her on like giants' palms outspread. The strong, unfaltering breeze was so full that sky and air seemed vast outbellying sails; the whole world boomed before the wind.

Long maintaining an enchanted silence, Ahab stood apart; and every time the pitching ship lowered her bowsprit, he turned to eye the bright sun's rays ahead; and when she profoundly settled by the stern, he turned behind and saw the sun's rearward place, and how the same yellow rays were blending with his undeviating wake.

"Ha, ha, my ship! You might well be taken now for the sea-chariot of the sun. Ho, ho! All you nations before my prow, I bring the sun to you! Yoke on the further billows; hallo! A tandem, I drive the sea!"
But suddenly reined back by some counter thought, he hurried toward the helm, huskily demanding how the ship was heading.
"East-southeast, sir," said the frightened steersman.
"You lie!" striking him with his clenched fist. "Heading east at this hour in the morning, and the sun astern?"
Upon this every soul was confounded; for the phenomenon just then observed by Ahab had unaccountably escaped everyone else; but its very blinding obviousness must have been the cause.

Thrusting his head halfway into the binnacle, Ahab caught one glimpse of the compasses; his uplifted arm slowly fell; for a moment he almost seemed to stagger. Standing behind him, Starbuck looked, and lo! The two compasses pointed east, and the Pequod was heading due west.

But before the first wild alarm could get out abroad among the crew, the old man with a rigid laugh exclaimed: "I have it! It has happened before. Mr. Starbuck, last night's thunder turned our compasses — that's all. You have before now heard of such a thing, I take it."
"Aye; but never before has it happened to me, sir," said the pale mate, gloomily.

Here it must be said that accidents like this have in more than one case occurred to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as developed in the mariner's needle, is, as all know, essentially one with the electricity seen in heaven; hence it is not to be much marveled at that such things should happen. In instances where the lightning has actually struck the vessel, as well as those where the storm merely rages without direct contact, the compasses have been known to be completely reversed.

Deliberately standing before the binnacle, and eyeing the reversed compasses, the old man, with the sharp of his extended hand, now took the precise bearing of the sun, and satisfied that the needles were exactly inverted, shouted out his orders for the ship's course to be changed accordingly. The yards were braced hard up, and once more the Pequod thrust her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposed fair one had only been luring her on to her doom.

Meanwhile, whatever were his own secret thoughts, Starbuck said nothing but quietly issued all requisite orders; while Stubb and Flask — who in some small degree seemed then to be sharing his feelings — likewise silently acquiesced. As for the rest of the crew, though some of them grumbled, their obedience of habit carried them through.
For a space the old man walked the deck in rolling reveries. But chancing to slip with his ivory heel, he saw the crushed copper sight-tubes of the quadrant he had the day before dashed to the deck.

"You poor, proud heaven-gazer and sun's pilot! Yesterday I wrecked you, and today the compasses would fain have wrecked me. So, so. But Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. Mr. Starbuck — a lance without a pole; a top-maul, and the smallest of the sail-maker's needles. Quick!"

Contributing, perhaps, to the impulse behind what he was now about to do were certain prudent motives, whose aim might have been to revive the spirits of his crew by a stroke of his subtle skill, in a matter so wondrous as that of the inverted compasses. Besides, the old man well knew that to steer by transpointed needles, though feasible enough, was not a thing to be passed over without complaint by his officers.

"Men," said he, steadily turning upon the crew, as the mate handed him the things he had demanded, "my men, the thunder turned old Ahab's needles; but out of this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his own, that will point as true as any."
Abashed glances of servile wonder were exchanged by the sailors, as this was said; and with fascinated eyes they awaited whatever magic might follow. But Starbuck looked away.

With a blow from the top-maul Ahab knocked off the steel head of the lance, and then handing to the mate the long iron rod remaining, bade him hold it upright, without its touching the deck. Then, with the maul, after repeatedly smiting the upper end of this iron rod, he placed the blunted needle endwise on the top of it, and less strongly hammered that, several times. All the while, the crew was intently watching, their mouths open. Then turning the needle in the opposite direction, he held it before him, swung it back and forth, and cried: "Look!" — for it slowly settled to the east, the very direction the compasses had pointed before.
One after another they peered in, for nothing but their own eyes could persuade such ignorance as theirs, and one after another they slunk away.
In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.
